Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for drafting OMIM phenotype entries with one LLM (Claude Opus 5.5) from exactly the 2-12 papers the curators cited, with the causal gene withheld. Model, guards, claim-level audit and scoring are held fixed so that only the generation strategy varies: direct long-context reading, an agentic curator, two extract-then-write pipelines (evidence graph, case table), recall-then-verify, a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, learned curation guide, reconciled case database). The primary endpoint is coverage of fact lists split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar (476 paragraphs, 6,652 facts); secondary measures are HPO synopsis F1, variant recall/precision, causal-gene F1 and inheritance. Findings: (1) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (paired +43.7 points on 46 entries), and most missed facts are absent from the supplied text; (2) on 93 entries all strategies completed, the reading strategies lie within 47.2-49.1%, near a measured replicate-noise half-width of 1.0 point, with only the case table clearly lower; (3) strategies separate observationally where more full text is readable (21 entries), and a matched ablation attributes much of the case-table gap to extraction effort; (4) memory-first strategies reach about 15%; (5) the audit flags 60/60 planted single-fact errors and 0/60 unaltered re-audits. Every judgement is made by the generator's own model family, with no human validation.
Strengths: Well-controlled design (all three reviewers): sources fixed to the curators' reference list, shared model, guards, audit and scoring, causal gene withheld, so the generation strategy is the only variable. This isolates the question better than most RAG / long-context / graph comparisons, which also vary retrieval.

The within-paper access manipulation (Section 4.1, Figure 2) is a clean paired experiment on the same papers and the same 2,120 fixed facts, reported before and after repair, with every missed and conveyed fact attributed against the available text (Figure 3, Table 16). It turns an expected direction into a measured effect size.

Unusually disciplined statistics: paired bootstrap intervals, better/worse/tied counts, sign tests with Holm correction, a replicate-noise floor from three regenerations on 30 entries (Table 17; the arithmetic checks out), judge variation, and an explicit statement that a single run cannot rank the reading strategies.
Fact lists are fixed once before any draft is seen, removing a draft-dependent denominator; the paper shows that re-splitting per draft inflates levels by 2-5 points.

Completion is treated as an outcome: the safety-filter asymmetry between one-call and per-paper strategies is identified, an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis is reported (Table 7), and a spurious 2.1-point deficit from an earlier rule is openly corrected. Table 2 lists every experiment with its entry set and dropouts.
The matched ablation (Section 4.6) separates representation from extraction effort, so the case table is not blamed for a deficit partly caused by a lower-effort extractor.

Contamination is taken seriously (memory-only control by creation era; held-out entries created June-November 2026), and negative results (recall-then-verify, learned guide, reconciliation) are reported.

Limitations are candid and specific (24% of draft statements have a reference counterpart; the audit checks fidelity, not correctness); costs and token counts are reported and the harness and per-entry outputs are to be released.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement (raised by all three reviewers as the most important gap). Drafting, fact splitting, coverage judging, auditing and provenance attribution all use one model family, so 79.8% vs 36.1%, the 1.7% 'stated in no supplied text', and 60/60 are model-judged quantities; replicate and judge variation measure precision, not validity, and self-preference bias (cited by the authors) could favour some strategies. A curator/expert sample of 100-300 fact judgements and audit verdicts, or a second judge family on a subset, is expected for a benchmark contribution.

Single proprietary model, one run per entry, CLI without temperature or seed control. Whether the closeness of reading strategies holds for other model families, or for weaker/smaller-context models where extraction or agentic reading might help more, is untested; exact regeneration is not reproducible.

Narrow regime: 2-12 references, inputs that fit one prompt, 19% full text, reference lists given to every strategy. This is precisely where direct long-context reading is expected to be hard to beat; the regime where graph and agentic designs should matter (30-75 references, inputs beyond the context window, retrieval) is a 10-entry exploratory appendix, and retrieval is checked on ten entries.

The primary endpoint is narrow and indirect: only variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs are scored, matching about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements. Strategies may differ on phenotype narrative, cross-paper synthesis or organisation that the endpoint does not see, so the null between reading strategies may partly reflect the endpoint; secondary measures only partly fill the gap.

The headline access effect is largely expected by construction (curators wrote from full papers), as the authors acknowledge; its value lies in the effect size and attribution, not in a surprising finding. Coverage restricted to facts stated in the supplied text would be a more sensitive test of reading quality.

The 'strategies separate where more full text is readable' claim (abstract, Section 4.3, conclusion) rests on 21 entries in an observational grouping confounded with era and journal, and is not reconciled with the controlled check: in the matched ablation the evidence graph is +1.0 / +1.8 against direct reading on 40 full-text-weighted entries, while Figure 4 / Table 12 show -1.8 in the 'half or more full text' group. The ablation also makes two changes together, so attributing the case-table gain to extraction effort is an inference. The claim is presented more strongly than the evidence supports.

The 'replicate-noise half-width' (1.0 point) is used as a threshold for meaningful differences without explaining its relation to the bootstrap interval over entries, which already absorbs run-to-run variability; comparing point estimates against it is not a calibrated test. The evidence graph minus direct reading is +0.7 on the 30-entry replicate subset but -0.5 on the 93 entries, which is not discussed.

Audit validation is weak as a test: planted errors are single rule-based value swaps (count, zygosity, residue, inheritance) in paragraphs the audit had already passed; omissions, misattributed citations, cross-paper conflation and unsupported generalisations are untested, so 60/60 should not be read as audit sensitivity.

Limited ML novelty and relevance for the ICLR main track: no new method; all strategies are the authors' own implementations, and no published system (PaperQA2, GraphRAG, STORM) is run under the same guards to anchor them; the general measurement lessons are good practice rather than new. The audience may be closer to biocuration or a datasets-and-benchmarks track.

Presentation is very dense and heavily hedged: a hard-to-parse title, an abstract packed with numbers and qualifiers, key definitions (fact lists, in-scope paragraphs, 'partly present') spread across sections and appendix, and repeated switching between means over entries and pooled-over-facts figures (36.1% vs 31.2%; 79.8% vs 77.3/77.4%). Figure 2 shows pooled after-repair values (77.4%, +43.9) while the text leads with means before repair (79.8%, +43.7).

Minor reporting issues: the Section 4.1 provenance sentence lists 1,061+222+102+24 = 1,409 of 1,420 facts, omitting the 11 (0.8%) category present in Table 16; Table 7 and other appendix tables render '<0.001' as a stray glyph; the access strata in Figure 4 / Table 12 (46/25/21) sum to 92 of 93 entries and the remaining entry is not explained; Table 1 reports variant precision 100.0% for recall-then-verify on n=23 without a caveat.
Questions: Can you provide human validation on a sample (100-300 items judged by a geneticist or OMIM-style curator, stratified by strategy) of fact splitting, present/partly/absent judgements, audit verdicts and 'stated in available text' attributions, and report agreement and any strategy-dependent bias?

Can you re-judge a subset (e.g., the 30-entry replicate subset) with a different model family, and/or regenerate with a second generator family or a smaller-context model, to check whether the access effect and the closeness of reading strategies hold?

How do the 21 'half or more full text' entries of Figure 4 relate to the 40 matched-ablation entries, and which estimate of the evidence-graph effect where full text is plentiful (-1.8 or +1.0/+1.8) should readers take? Can an extra ablation arm separate extraction effort from writer-chosen synopsis terms and inheritance?

How should the replicate-noise half-width be interpreted relative to the bootstrap CI? Would a mixed-effects model with entry and replicate as random effects on the 30 replicated entries give a more principled interval? Why does the evidence graph lead on the 30-entry subset but trail on the 93?

What is coverage when restricted to facts stated in the supplied text, or to full-text papers only, where strategies can actually differ? How sensitive are the paired differences to dropping half credit for 'partly present'?

Have you run any strategy on inputs exceeding one prompt (the 30-75-reference tier) with enough entries to compare paradigms, and why were published systems (PaperQA2, GraphRAG) not run under the same guards?
Does the memory-only control's ability to name the causal gene (F1 about 84%) interact with strategy differences, e.g. by priming what the writer extracts?
What happens to the 11 abstract-only conveyed facts missing from the Section 4.1 breakdown, and what is the single entry outside the three access strata?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section is thorough and candid: one model family, no human validation, narrow reference, open-access text without supplements, reference list given to every strategy, single-prompt regime, small post-development sample, stopped replies, audit untested on omissions.

Not sufficiently emphasised: the closeness of strategies may partly reflect the judge sharing the generator's family; results may not transfer to retrieval or larger-corpus settings where design choices are expected to matter most; the planted-error test covers only the easiest error type; the observational full-text separation conflicts with the matched ablation for the evidence graph.
Societal risk (machine-generated text mistaken for curated clinical content) is addressed in the ethics statement.
Thought: Three reviewers converge (all Overall 5, Confidence 4, Reject; Soundness 3, Presentation 2, Contribution 2; Originality 2/2/3). Consensus strengths: tight experimental control, a clean within-paper access manipulation, honest statistics and completion handling. Consensus blockers: zero human validation with the generator's own family as judge, a single model, an expected headline effect plus a null in a narrow single-prompt regime, a narrow endpoint, and a 'separation' claim that is observational and unreconciled with the ablation. I checked the paper text: the 1,409/1,420 gap is the 11 (0.8%) category present in Table 16 but omitted from the prose; Table 12 strata sum to 92 of 93; the evidence graph is -1.8 in the top stratum vs +1.0/+1.8 in the ablation. Rigor is real but validity and significance are not yet established for ICLR. Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly say human validation plus a second model/judge family could move them to weak accept. Reject, persuadable.
